item.title: DistroKid Removes Music Following Universal Music Group AI Slop Lawsuit
item.description:
DistroKid Removes Music Following Universal Music Group AI Slop Lawsuit

DistroKid has begun unceremoniously removing songs from its platform without providing notice or explanations to affected artists. The distributor confirmed to The Verge that these takedowns are a direct response to claims made by Universal Music Group (UMG), which filed a lawsuit in September alleging that DistroKid has created an “AI-slop pipeline.” While the company states it is responding to UMG’s claims, artists report that original, non-AI works are being caught up in the purge.

⚙️ Key Details

  • DistroKid is taking down songs in response to a lawsuit filed by UMG in September.
  • Amanda Ferri, DistroKid’s VP of Artist Services, stated that a “very small number of recordings” have been removed and that the company “strongly dispute[s]” UMG’s allegations.
  • DistroKid aims to minimize disruption while protecting the ability of artists to release music, despite reports of removals occurring without warning.

🧩 Impacted Artists

Multiple musicians have reported the removal of original works that do not utilize AI, often with no communication before or after the tracks were taken down.

Artist Impacted Work Reported Issues
McGwire Six songs Included a licensed cover and a marketplace beat; one song was flagged for a sample released two years after the track itself.
Insane Ian Original song Removed with no warning and no explanation provided by the company.
King Chase Entire album An album online for 3-4 years without incident or copyright strikes was removed.

💡 Why it matters

The purge has highlighted significant frustrations regarding DistroKid’s transparency and support systems:

  • Artists report having to contact the company themselves to find out why their music was removed, often navigating “lengthy circular conversation[s]” with bots before reaching a live agent.
  • Music producer Jesse Cannon stated that DistroKid “gave up on customer service about two years ago,” treating it as a “waste of profits” due to their high market share.
  • Former employees reportedly told Cannon that the company does not provide a mechanism for artists to have recourse or a warning to debate takedown claims.
  • Much of the artist frustration stems from a lack of communication and the difficulty of contacting DistroKid agents.

#DistroKid #UMG #MusicStreaming #ArtificialIntelligence #Lawsuit

Source: DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit

item.title: Apple Settles Class Action Lawsuit Over AI-Upgraded Siri Rollout Delays
item.description:
Apple Settles Class Action Lawsuit Over AI-Upgraded Siri Rollout Delays

Apple has agreed to a $250 million settlement to resolve claims that the company failed to deliver an AI-upgraded version of Siri as expected. While Apple denies any wrongdoing, the settlement allows eligible iPhone owners to submit claims for a payout.

⚙️ Key details

The class action lawsuit alleged that Apple established a clear consumer expectation that AI features showcased at WWDC 2024 would be available upon the launch of the iPhone 16. Although marketed as “built for Apple Intelligence,” the devices launched with a more limited set of capabilities. The promised AI-upgraded Siri was subsequently delayed and only released recently with iOS 27.

🚀 Eligibility and Claims

Individuals who purchased specific iPhone models in the United States between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, are eligible to participate. To file a claim, users must provide their name, contact information, and device serial number on the settlement website by December 21, 2026.

Eligible Device Model
iPhone 15 Pro
iPhone 15 Pro Max
iPhone 16 models

💰 Payout Information

The estimated payout is $25 per eligible device. However, this amount may increase to as much as $95 depending on the total volume of claims submitted.

#Apple #Siri #AppleIntelligence #ClassAction #Lawsuit

Source: iPhone owners can now submit claims in Apple’s $250 million Siri AI settlement

item.title: Anthropic Faces Class Action Lawsuit Over Allegedly Misleading Claude Max Subscription Limits
item.description:
Anthropic Faces Class Action Lawsuit Over Allegedly Misleading Claude Max Subscription Limits

Anthropic is facing legal scrutiny after subscribers accused the company of deceptively marketing its premium Claude Max AI subscription tier. The expanded class action lawsuit alleges that Anthropic misrepresented usage limits, leaving customers feeling misled about the value of their $100-$200 monthly subscriptions.

🔍 Overview

Claude subscribers claim Anthropic obscured critical usage restrictions for its Max plan, advertising “5x” or “20x” greater capacity than the base Pro tier while burying strict session-based limits in hard-to-find fine print. The lawsuit argues this constitutes false advertising.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Pricing Tiers:
    Plan Cost Advertised Usage Actual Limit (Alleged)
    Max 5x $100/month 5× Pro capacity 5-hour sessions with weekly cap
    Max 20x $200/month 20× Pro capacity Same session/weekly constraints
  • Hidden Limitations: The complaint states session limits were added months after launch and required clicking multiple hyperlinks to discover, with one user comparing it to “a bigger gas tank with a restricted fuel pump.”
  • Corporate Priority: Anthropic deprioritized other applications (e.g., OpenClaw) to focus on power users, yet allegedly obscured Max plan constraints.

💬 Key Quotes

  • Reddit User: “The weekly allowance is what the pricing page makes you think you’re buying. The rolling 5-hour window is what actually controls whether you can work.”
  • Attorney Monica Vaca: “People see that they are going to get this dramatically expanded usage… but when they sign up, they are surprised that they’re not getting the usage that they thought they were getting.”
  • Anthropic’s Defense: “Accessing this clarifying information required nothing more than clicking hyperlinks… the digital equivalent of flipping a product over to read the back label.”

⚖️ Legal Context

  • Filed by former FTC attorneys Monica Vaca and Kati Daffan (38 combined years at the agency), the lawsuit emphasizes false advertising principles: “You can’t lie when you’re marketing a product.”
  • Plaintiffs argue Anthropic violated consumer protection laws through deliberate obscurity of terms, forcing a “buyer beware” dynamic for premium subscribers.

💡 Why It Matters

This case represents a rare legal challenge to AI industry pricing practices, highlighting tensions between profit models and transparency. As AI tools become essential for professionals, unclear usage policies risk eroding trust—particularly when upgrades cost $100-$200 monthly. The outcome could pressure companies to simplify terms and align marketing with actual user experience.

#Anthropic #ClaudeAI #Lawsuit #AIEthics #ConsumerRights

Source: A new class action lawsuit questions whether Anthropic broke the law by misleading power users
